evidence.text: The file description identifies a digitally created SVG depicting 字 in Shang bronze-script style. It names the Sinica database among its sources, specifies the 字父己觶 (late Shang), and states CC0 1.0 for the image. This is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph or rubbing.
evidence.title: File:字-bronze-shang.svg

evidence.source: Taiwan Digital Archives and Digital Learning Program
evidence.text: The catalog lists 字父己觶 as a Shang-cast ink rubbing (商鑄墨拓本), identifier 金0442. This supports a Shang-period inscriptional witness, but the opened page is a catalog listing, not an independent paleographic reading or a securely dated use of the word.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Revised Mandarin Dictionary
evidence.text: The entry gives Mandarin zì; lists ‘written character/sign recording language’ and older senses including a personal courtesy name, a contract/document, betrothal of a woman, nurture, and love. These are dictionary senses, not a dated chronology of their development.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Revised Mandarin Dictionary
evidence.text: The entry gives 子 readings zǐ and neutral-tone zi; the child/offspring sense is associated with zǐ. Current Mandarin readings are not evidence by themselves for an ancient sound relation.

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction dataset
evidence.text: The authors describe their dataset columns and note that reconstructions for unattested pre-Qin words may represent hypothesized readings. The official project PDF was inspected, but its searchable text did not expose the 子 and 字 entries; the local dossier’s exact TSV entries remain locally reported rather than independently checked against a public upstream row in this run.

evidence.text: The guide explains that the database organizes ancient forms and that its bronze forms generally come from CHANT, with vessel name, period, and corpus identifier shown for each selected form. The 字 entry timed out, so this guide does not establish the entry’s particular interpretation or forms.

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project search result quoting 段玉裁《說文解字注》
evidence.field: 字 entry; commentary on senses and formation
evidence.text: The search result reports 段玉裁’s account: 字 originally means giving birth, extended to nurturing and then to written characters; it also reproduces 許慎’s ‘乳也。从子在宀下，子亦聲’ and preface explanation that characters multiply by derivation. This is a transmitted Han lexicographic analysis and later commentary, not independent confirmation of the graphic interpretation or a dated semantic path. Opening the page returned 403.
evidence.title: 說文解字注 — Chinese Text Project

evidence.source: 東亞漢學研究 2019 special issue paper, search result
evidence.text: The result notes that scholarly discussion of the ancient graph’s form and meaning continues and that some scholars have challenged the 說文 explanation ‘從子在宀下’. The PDF was not readable on open in this run, so the competing analyses cannot be summarized or evaluated from this result alone.
evidence.title: 《東亞漢學研究》2019 年特別號

gaps: The 字父己觶 catalog listing supports a Late Shang graph witness, but no inspected inscriptional publication supplied a secure absolute date or contextual reading; the catalog listing does not establish that this is the earliest attestation.

No securely dated early use of 字 for ‘give birth/nurture’ versus ‘written character’ was located. The dictionary gloss ordering and 說文/段注 account do not independently date semantic change. The link between the senses remains an ancient lexicographic explanation, with alternative analyses still unresolved.

The dossier’s common analysis of 宀 as roof/semantic element and 子 as phonetic (and perhaps semantic) is supported here only as the reported 說文 analysis; there was no accessible independent character-specific paleographic study. A research result signals disagreement, but its PDF could not be inspected.

Modern readings verified from Taiwan MOE are 子 zǐ and 字 zì. The exact local Unihan rows were not available in this invocation; both official per-character Unicode lookup URLs returned internal errors, so no Unihan click-through claim is made.

The Baxter–Sagart project PDF was inspected, but its precise rows were not recoverable by search. Do not silently equate dossier transcriptions with the project PDF; the local TSV notation *[ts]əʔ / *tsəʔ for 子 and *mə-dzə(ʔ)-s for 字 remains a local-only report awaiting an exact upstream row check.

Commons description indicates the selected-style candidate is a modern digital redraw and grants CC0, but tool open repeatedly failed and no exact original image URL was verified. Therefore no image candidate is returned. The Sinica page also describes CC0 query-image rights, but its specific 字 image label and direct image URL were not verified.

No evidence for graph corruption or miscopying was established. No whole-graph phonetic borrowing claim was found; 子 is discussed as a proposed sound component within 字. Claims about Proto-Sino-Tibetan cognates and cross-language cognacy remain unverified here.

limitations.text: No image is proposed because although Commons search exposed an exact file description page, the page could not be opened to copy its original image link. Direct-image attempts were inaccessible, and the file URL cannot be guessed. The page describes it as a modern digital SVG redraw in Shang bronze style, sourced in part from Sinica, and gives CC0 1.0; however exact image-link verification failed. The archive catalog listing 字父己觶 (金0442) is a usable lead for an actual rubbing record but its item page failed, and rights and direct image URL were not established.

The available source asserts a Late Shang bronze example but does not provide a precise absolute date or enough contextual text to connect the graph to a specific spoken sense. It should be captioned as a period-style/form witness rather than evidence that ‘written character’ or ‘birth/nurture’ was its earliest sense.
